sections.title: 3. ARE: Scaling Up Agent Environments and Evaluations
5.2 Time Reveals the Impact of Inference Speed

abstract_sentences.text: We introduce Gaia2, a benchmark for evaluating large language model agents in realistic, asynchronous environments.

evidence.anchor: a benchmark for evaluating large language model agents

abstract_sentences.text: Unlike prior static or synchronous evaluations, Gaia2 introduces scenarios where environments evolve independently of agent actions, requiring agents to operate under temporal constraints, adapt to noisy and dynamic events, resolve ambiguity, and collaborate with other agents.

evidence.anchor: environments evolve independently of agent actions

abstract_sentences.text: Each scenario is paired with a write-action verifier, enabling fine-grained, action-level evaluation and making Gaia2 directly usable for reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.

Our evaluation of state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source models shows that no model dominates across capabilities: GPT-5 (high) reaches the strongest overall score of 42% pass@1 but fails on time-sensitive tasks, Claude-4 Sonnet trades accuracy and speed for cost, Kimi-K2 leads among open-source models with 21% pass@1.
These results highlight fundamental trade-offs between reasoning, efficiency, robustness, and expose challenges in closing the ‘sim2real’ gap.
Gaia2 is built on a consumer environment with the open-source Agents Research Environments platform and designed to be easy to extend.

By releasing Gaia2 alongside the foundational ARE framework, we aim to provide the community with a flexible infrastructure for developing, benchmarking, and training the next generation of practical agent systems.

experimental_design.name: Numbered research questions and stopping rule
experimental_design.description: No numbered RQ, pre-registration, minimum effect, or stopping rule appears; the later Performance drivers paragraph gives two observational hypotheses.

experimental_design.name: Core and augmented scenario counts
experimental_design.description: The paper states 800 unique core human-authored scenarios, a 160-scenario Gaia2-mini subset, and two augmentation setups adding 320 scenarios for 1,120 total.

evidence.anchor: adding 320 scenarios to the original 800 for a total of 1,120 scenarios

experimental_design.name: Capability allocation
experimental_design.description: The five core splits are Execution, Search, Ambiguity, Adaptability, and Time; Appendix B.1.2 states 160 scenarios per capability split. Noise and A2A are environment-level modifiers.

experimental_design.name: Human annotation protocol
experimental_design.description: Annotators explore generated Mobile universes, create write-action/event DAG ground truth, undergo independent multi-round validation and consistency checks, and use automated guardrails plus post-hoc baseline difficulty calibration.

evidence.anchor: multiple rounds of validation by independent annotators

experimental_design.name: Mobile universe and app/tool surface
experimental_design.description: Mobile has 12 apps and 101 tools; synthetic persona data are propagated through a dependency graph, and each universe has 400K–800K tokens excluding filesystem contents.

experimental_design.name: Dynamic event and observability design
experimental_design.description: Events are timestamped and scheduled absolutely or relatively through DAGs; low/medium/high notification policies control which environment events reach the agent, with medium as Gaia2 default.

experimental_design.name: Capability task design
experimental_design.description: Execution chains writes, Search chains reads, Ambiguity asks for clarification, Adaptability reacts to dependent Env events, Time enforces deadlines, A2A replaces apps with app-agents, and Noise injects tool/environment perturbations.

experimental_design.name: ReAct baseline
experimental_design.description: All models use the same model-agnostic ReAct scaffold: one structured JSON tool call per step, pre-step notification injection, and post-step termination checking.

evidence.anchor: one tool call per step in structured JSON

experimental_design.name: Model and inference settings
experimental_design.description: Evaluations use full context (>=128K), temperature 0.5, 16K token generation per turn, and three runs per scenario; termination is at 200 steps, context overflow, verification completion, or timeout.

evidence.anchor: All LLMs are evaluated at full context length

experimental_design.name: Time simulation and deployment handling
experimental_design.description: Generation latency consumes simulated time; outages/rate limits are handled by pausing and resuming with a matching offset. Time is additionally evaluated in instant mode.

experimental_design.name: Verifier metric and oracle
experimental_design.description: The verifier compares agent write actions with a minimal oracle sequence across consistency, causality, timing, and completeness; read actions are not penalized or matched.

experimental_design.name: Randomness and seed reporting
experimental_design.description: ARE claims deterministic execution with a fixed start state and seed, but the core experiment reports only three runs and does not list per-scenario seeds or run-level values.

evidence.anchor: deterministically given a fixed starting state and seed
with three runs to account for potential variance

experimental_design.name: Uncertainty reporting
experimental_design.description: Table 2 contains an unlabeled ± spread; Table 3 explicitly says standard error. Most figures do not define ribbons or error bars.

evidence.anchor: three runs to account for potential variance

experimental_design.name: Human and verifier validation
experimental_design.description: The verifier is validated on 450 hand-labeled trajectories; the paper also says an average human annotator solved every task but was slower using ARE GUI.

final_judgment.single_storyline: ARE turns static final-outcome agent evaluation into event-based, time-driven Mobile scenarios with selective notifications and an action-level write oracle; Gaia2 then uses this controlled causal chain to expose capability-specific trade-offs (pp.2–6).
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The body keeps the ARE pipeline, seven capability taxonomy, verifier aggregate validation, complete split score table, and Time/A2A mechanism plots, enough to decide what is evaluated, how success is judged, and why model rankings differ (pp.3–10).
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Appendix A–B moves event lifecycle, notification whitelists, universe generation, GUI, annotation guardrails, oracle matching, judge hacking, provider handling, PTC, and noise checks; this preserves conceptual self-sufficiency but makes verifier and deployment boundaries appendix-dependent (pp.15–32).
final_judgment.best_pattern: A closed-loop Figure 2 first maps environment, event, notification, agent, and verification; Figure 4 maps that abstraction to capabilities; Table 2 and Figures 8–10 then move from broad score to time, cost, and collaboration mechanism (pp.3–10).
final_judgment.largest_gap: Overall score is a split average with no scenario denominator, Table 2 ± and Figure 10 ribbons lack definitions, Figure 7 reports correlation without a coefficient, and the sim2real claim has no real deployment test; critical verifier/scaffold caveats arrive in the appendix (pp.7–10, 19, 26–32).
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For dynamic agent benchmarks, design time progression, external events, observability, write commitments, and verification as one event-log causal chain; report capability-specific outcomes beside any overall score and preserve exploration freedom by excluding reads from write-oracle matching (pp.5–6, 16–18, 26–27).
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule fits simulable domains with logged events and a defensible minimal write oracle. Open-ended preferences, equivalent write traces, real service outages, unresolved cross-app temporal semantics, and genuinely concurrent actions require state-equivalence checks, real-world tests, or concurrent orchestration before Gaia2-style pass@1 is generalized (pp.8, 19, 27, 30–31).
